arctic.heroSubtitle: A data-driven story of sea-ice decline by Lukas Kreibig
arctic.heroLine1: The Arctic is warming nearly four times as fast as the rest of the world
arctic.heroLine2: Sea-ice melt is no longer a forecast
arctic.heroLine3: Scientists expect ice-free Arctic summers before 2050

geographic.title: How the Ice Is Vanishing
geographic.intro: In the Arctic, sea ice is not just scenery. For many places it is route, workplace, and risk. What changes when that season becomes shorter and harder to trust?

greenland.title: Greenland
greenland.description: The world's largest island is mostly ice sheet. Along the rocky coast, deep fjords cut inland and create sheltered places where people have lived with the Arctic sea for millennia.

uummannaqBay.title: Uummannaq Bay
uummannaqBay.description: 600 kilometers north of the Arctic Circle, this bay opens into one of Greenland's most dramatic fjord systems. In winter, the sea itself becomes the road.

uummannaqIsland.title: Uummannaq Island
uummannaqIsland.description: About 1,300 people live here beneath a distinctive heart-shaped mountain. In Uummannaq, ice is not scenery. It is mobility, timing, and safety.
uummannaqIsland.changing: The question is how that reliability is changing.

heartOfSeal.title: Heart of a Seal
heartOfSeal.description: Uummannaq takes its name from the mountain known as the Heart of a Seal. Beneath it, the town sits between harbor, fjord, and winter routes.

winterMonths.description: When the fjord freezes, the map changes. Routes that do not exist in summer become possible by sled, snowmobile, or on foot, but only while the ice can be trusted.

fishing.description: Fishing still shapes Uummannaq. But the story is not only climate loss: ice conditions, harbor access, markets, boats, and deliberate ice breakup all affect daily life.

voices.title: Voices from Uummannaq
voices.description: In the Life on Thin Ice study, residents describe how winter ice, travel, hunting, and fishing are changing. Their observations are where this measurement begins.
voices.learnMoreLink: Find out more about the study "Life on thin ice"
voices.learnMoreContent: The study: Bishop, B., Hansen, J., Kokelj, S. V. et al. (2017): “Life on thin ice: Insights from Uummannaq, Greenland for connecting climate science with Arctic communities”, Polar Science 13, pp. 60–75. Every verbatim quote in this story comes from that published paper. It connects fieldwork in Uummannaq Bay with a review of sea-ice research. Interviews and a focus group show why predictable winter ice matters for hunting, fishing, and travel, and why coastal ice thickness is underrepresented in mainstream research. Newer work on co-production adds an important caution: local ice change is not a single-cause story. Fishing, harbor access, deliberate ice breakup, modernization, and local knowledge all shape how ice is used and experienced.

quotes.iceDisappears:
When I was a child,
the ice was gone in June or July.
Now it is gone in April or May.
quotes.unstableClimate:
The most important change is the less stable weather.
The wind has become stronger
and harder to predict.
quotes.motorsledge:
Many hunters now prefer snowmobiles to dog sleds.
The winters are shorter,
and the catch has to move faster.
quotes.source: from the "Life on Thin Ice" study

measurement.title: Only a Feeling?
measurement.intro: But how do you test an observation like that? From above. For years, ESA's Sentinel-2 satellites have passed over Greenland and captured the fjord: image by image, winter by winter, until they add up to a comparable record.
measurement.step1: First, the view from above: this is Uummannaq as the satellite sees it.
measurement.step2: Now the raw winter image. Scenes like this are the basis for the measurement.
measurement.step3: Since 2017, ESA's Sentinel programme has provided regular images. Thousands of scenes have to become one consistent record.
measurement.step4: A computer-vision pipeline reads each image. It masks land and dense cloud, then separates ice from open water in what is left.
measurement.step5: The overlay is not the conclusion. What comes out is a single number per day: the share of the area that could be judged at all that day which the pipeline reads as ice. Land, cloud and data gaps are not in the denominator. A fjord frozen shore to shore under a clear sky therefore comes out at 100 percent, and a cloudy day is not marked down simply because there was cloud in the frame. That is the number every chart from here on shows.
measurement.learnMoreLink: Learn More about the Computer Vision Pipeline
measurement.learnMoreTitle: Computer Vision Pipeline for Sea Ice Detection
measurement.learnMoreContent:
Input: Sentinel-2 L1C (top-of-atmosphere reflectance, no atmospheric correction), all 13 bands, streamed from AWS. The analysed area is a fixed rectangle over Uummannaq Bay, roughly 14 by 18 kilometres, of which 253.5 km² is water, measured from the land mask. Season: mid-February to late June, day 45 to 181 of the year.

Processing, in this order:
1. All 13 bands are loaded onto a common 10 m grid; B11 (20 m) and the 60 m bands are upsampled to it.
2. The band stack is average-pooled over 4 by 4 pixels. Everything after this is decided on that 40 m grid, one cell covering 40 by 40 metres.
3. Cloud mask: a U-Net trained on the CloudSEN12 taxonomy outputs four classes. Exactly one of them is used, dense cloud, at probability 0.5 and above, then morphologically closed. Thin cloud and cloud shadow stay unflagged.
4. Land mask: a static coastline excludes rock and tundra. Pixels with no signal, the black image borders, are flagged too.
5. Ice/water: NDSI = (B3 − B11)/(B3 + B11), NDWI = (B3 − B8)/(B3 + B8).
   Solid ice NDSI > 0.52 · thin or wet ice 0.31 to 0.52 · open water NDWI > 0.25.

What the published number is: the share of ice in the area that could actually be judged that day. The denominator is not the whole grid but the clear water surface, with land, cloud and data gaps taken out. A frozen fjord under a clear sky comes out at 100%.

Until recently the whole grid sat in that denominator, and it mattered. A cell classified as cloud can never also be ice, so every cloud lowers the value whatever lies beneath it. That would be tolerable if cloud were spread evenly across the years. It is not: over the analysed window mean cloud cover rises from 0.149 in the 2017 to 2020 seasons to 0.273 in the 2021 to 2025 ones. The old denominator turned that near doubling of cloudiness into ice loss. On the same data the measured decline between the early and late periods drops from 32.4 to 23.4 percent. For scale, the other analysis choices barely register: season window and averaging method move the answer by less than a percentage point, the denominator by ten.

The price is coverage. A scene that saw less than 30% of the fjord is not a measurement of it and is dropped rather than averaged in. That is 432 of the 1552 scenes, or 27.8%, including 257 whose class shares sum past the grid.

What this method cannot do:
• It resolves nothing below 40 metres. Narrow leads and cracks vanish in the pooling, and a cell that is half ice and half water falls to one side on its average.
• Cloud detection is unreliable, and the change of denominator fixes only the mechanical half of that. Thin cloud and cloud shadow are never flagged at all in this vintage of the data and pass straight into the ice/water decision. No denominator helps against cloud the model failed to see.
• Melt ponds sit as water on top of ice. They read as open water and tend to date the measured breakup earlier. This bias points the same way as the result and grows in warm springs.
• The season starts in mid-February because the sun is too low before that. February rests on few usable scenes under very low sun and long mountain shadows.
• 53.3% of the days in the window shown have a usable scene of their own. The rest are filled from neighbouring days or from the day-of-year mean and are marked as such in the calendar chart. 2017 is the thinnest season at 26.7%; since 2019 no season falls below 48.5%. These shares were higher before the denominator was corrected, because scenes that barely saw the fjord still counted then. The curves also show a centred 7-day mean.
• A first comparison against Sentinel-1 radar, which needs neither sunlight nor a clear sky, has been run, but it answers one question only. On the late winter days when the optical chain reports almost no ice under an almost clear sky, radar backscatter sits in the range of confirmed fast ice rather than of open water, in both well sampled viewing geometries. That bounds an error; it does not calibrate the record. The ice fraction itself and the break-up date remain unvalidated, and radar and optical both read melt water on ice as water.

The daily values are published as CSV: /data/summary_test_cleaned.csv

How certain is this decline?

Not certain enough to call it established. The exact permutation test over all 126 possible splits of the nine seasons gives p = 0.12. Tested for a monotone trend, by Mann-Kendall, p = 0.35. Before the denominator was corrected the same test gave p = 0.03, but that was the weather artefact rather than the ice: a correction that weakens a claim is still a correction.

Three numbers say why. The spread between the years of the later period (standard deviation 0.21) is larger than the difference between the two period means (0.20). The 2022 season, at 0.94, sits above three of the four early years. And there are nine winters.

How sensitive is the figure to the analysis?

Move the period boundary and the measured decline runs from 6.8% (from 2022) to 24.9% (from 2019). Move the season window and it runs from 16.7% (day 60 to 120) to 25.3% (day 100 to 151). In none of those combinations does p fall below 0.07.

And one limitation that only surfaced while checking: 2017 and 2018 were taken mostly on the neighbouring tile 21WXU, everything from 2019 on tile 22WDD. Those two early years happen to carry the highest values, averaging 0.94 against 0.79 for 2019 and 2020. Using only years from the same tile, so from 2019 onwards, the decline falls to 15.7% at p = 0.48. Part of the effect could therefore be the change of tile rather than the ice, and this archive cannot separate the two.

What holds: the direction is the same under every defensible analysis. The certainty is not.

pixelInspector.title: From Image to Evidence
pixelInspector.raw: The satellite image is still a photograph of light. It has texture, shadows, snow, water, and uncertainty.
pixelInspector.mask: The overlay turns that image into classes. It does not replace judgment; it makes the judgment visible.
pixelInspector.classification: Each classified pixel is small. Together, thousands of them become an estimate of ice cover for that scene.
pixelInspector.outputTitle: Then It Becomes a Time Series
pixelInspector.output: Only after the same procedure is repeated across many scenes can one winter be compared with another.

memoryMeasurement.title: Memory Meets Measurement
memoryMeasurement.build: Watch one season fill in: the ice forms in February, holds through spring, then breaks apart by June. Each mark is one day, most of them one satellite scene.
memoryMeasurement.dayTitle: One scene becomes one daily value
memoryMeasurement.day: This day is the bridge between the satellite image and the table: the pipeline estimates how much of the analysed frame is ice that day.
memoryMeasurement.season: The sequence shows how a winter builds, holds, and breaks apart.
memoryMeasurement.intro: Now all measured seasons are in view. Each row is one winter in Uummannaq; each small mark is one day.
memoryMeasurement.early: The winters of 2017 to 2020 are the comparison point, not a perfect past.
memoryMeasurement.late: The winters since 2021 carry the summary value, measured against those first four years. It is a guide to the shift, not the whole explanation.
memoryMeasurement.latest: One year alone is never the story. It matters because it belongs to the pattern around it.
memoryMeasurement.caveat: Clouds, missing scenes, and local use remain part of the uncertainty. Weather, fishing economics, harbor access, deliberate ice breakup, and local knowledge all shape what ice means in practice.

visualProof.title: Season by Season
visualProof.description: Each small chart shows one Uummannaq ice season from February to June. The point is not one dramatic year, but the rhythm across years.
visualProof.numbersDescription: The highlighted seasons from 2021 on sit lower in the same calendar window than the four winters before them.
visualProof.trend: Less ice in the measured season
visualProof.conclusion: The satellite record and local memory point the same way: earlier breakup, while leaving room for local causes and year-to-year variability.

newAbnormal.title: When "Normal" Shifts
newAbnormal.description: To make the shift legible, we compare the first four measured seasons with the later measured years.
newAbnormal.earlyPeriod: The blue line shows the 2017-2020 mean. The light band shows how much those years varied.
newAbnormal.livingOutside: The red line shows the 2021-2025 mean. In this comparison, the later years sit lower across much of the season.
newAbnormal.consequence: season mean (mid-February to late June) against 2017–2020
newAbnormal.result: That does not explain every local decision, and it is not yet proof: nine winters are too few to establish this difference statistically. The direction is the same under every defensible analysis. The certainty is not.

trajectory.title: A Direction, Not a Fate
trajectory.rate: The yearly record slopes downward. Treat the line as evidence of direction, not as a fixed date for the future.

recall.title: Back to the Opening Memory
recall.description: The story began with a memory that spans a lifetime: as a child, the ice held into June or July. Nine years of satellite data is far too short to test a childhood recollection. But it can ask the same question in numbers. Each dot is the day one Uummannaq winter's ice broke up.

shift.title: Earlier, on Average
shift.description: Across the measured years, breakup moved from a late-May average toward mid-May, about eleven days earlier. It is a short, nine-year window, so read it as a direction, not a fixed date.

unpredictable.title: And Harder to Predict
unpredictable.description: The bigger change is the swing: recent winters break up as early as late April or as late as June. That matches the other thing residents stressed: the season has become less stable and harder to trust. The satellite and the people on the ice describe one change from two sides: one measures the area, the other lives the risk.

future.trend: A shorter period of reliable ice changes the balance between ice roads, boats, harbor work, and safety decisions.
future.memory: For children in Uummannaq, ice is both inherited memory and a changing practical problem.
future.traditions: Dog teams, snowmobiles, boats, and local judgment now share a more unstable season.

toArctic.title: From Uummannaq to the Arctic
toArctic.description: Uummannaq shows one local shift. The Arctic-wide record gives the scale: winter maximums, summer minimums, old ice, and rapid regional warming.
toArctic.learnMoreTitle: Methodology & Data Sources – Arctic Sea Ice
toArctic.learnMoreContent:
This story draws on operational datasets from NASA, NOAA/NSIDC and Our World in Data. An automated Python pipeline pulls them in. How far each source actually reaches is listed in the credits under “State of the data”.

Data sources
NASA GISS – temperature anomalies: https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/
NOAA – daily Arctic sea-ice extent: https://nsidc.org/sea-ice-today
Our World in Data – global CO₂ emissions: https://ourworldindata.org/co2-and-greenhouse-gas-emissions

Processing steps
1. A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow triggers the update.
2. Latest CSV / JSON files are downloaded, validated and reshaped with Pandas.
3. Z-scores standardise temperature, ice extent and CO₂ to a common scale.
4. The cleaned dataset is written to data.json and served by FastAPI to the Next.js frontend.

arcticGlobe.title: What Summer Leaves Behind
arcticGlobe.description: At the end of each summer the sea ice pulls back to its yearly minimum. Seen from above, decade by decade, the loss is unmistakable: September ice has been shrinking by about 12 percent per decade since 1979, measured against the 1981–2010 September average.
arcticGlobe.intro: At the end of every summer the sea ice pulls back to its minimum. What is left has been measured without a gap since 1979.
arcticGlobe.decade1980: This is what September looked like in the 1980s: a closed sheet reaching far off the coasts of Canada and Siberia.
arcticGlobe.decade2000: Around the turn of the century the edge starts to give way. Where ice used to lie, the end of summer leaves open water.
arcticGlobe.decade2024: Today an area larger than Greenland is missing by the end of summer. The pale outline shows where the ice still stood in 1980.
arcticGlobe.attribution: September mean sea-ice extent (≥15 % concentration) · NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4
arcticGlobe.aria: Animated map: Arctic September sea ice shown on a 3-D globe. From 1980 to 2024 the ice cap visibly retreats; September ice has been shrinking by roughly 12 percent per decade since 1979, against the 1981–2010 September average. Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index.

seasonal.title: The Arctic Seasonal Record
seasonal.description: Each line traces one year of Arctic sea-ice extent, from autumn minimum to spring maximum and back again. Blue lines show older years, red lines show recent years.

early.title: 1979–2000: The Cold(er) Half
early.description: The first half of the record sits visibly higher. The ice had more room to recover through the year.

late.title: 2000 onward: The Recent Half
late.description: In the more recent years, the lines sit lower through much of the season.

current.title: Latest Available Year {{year}}
current.description: Finally, isolate {{year}} and compare it with the rest of the record.

breaking.title: Below the Earlier Range
breaking.description: Recent years often sit below the older envelope, especially around the winter maximum and late-summer minimum.

decades.title: Five Decades, One Direction
decades.description: Each colored band represents a decade of Arctic ice measurements. Watch them appear one by one and notice the unmistakable staircase downward. We open in the 1980s, which sit above the 1981–2010 average on every day of the year. The 1990s are the last decade that never once drops below that line.

1980s.title: The 1980s: The Old Normal
1980s.description: This soft blue band is our starting point, and it stays above the line all year. The 1980s run 0.34 to 0.97 million km² above the 1981–2010 average, with the widest surplus in late September.

1990s.title: The 1990s: First Cracks
1990s.description: The band drops but never crosses over. At 0.09 to 0.40 million km² above the average, the 1990s are the last decade that spends the whole year on the ice-rich side of the line.

2000s.title: The 2000s: A Lower Baseline
2000s.description: The curve moves below the line and stays there, every day of the year, 0.27 to 0.79 million km² short of the average. On 68 of those days the shortfall passes 0.6 million km².

2010s.title: The 2010s: Acceleration
2010s.description: The decline steepens. On 345 of 365 days the gap now exceeds 0.6 million km², the decade runs 1.07 million short across the year, and in early October it reaches 1.87 million.

2020s.title: The 2020s: A Lower Range
2020s.description: The current decade sits lowest of all: 1.21 million km² below the 1981–2010 average across the year, and 2.21 million short in mid October.
2020s.acceleration: The data shows no short-term return to the older range.

bridge.decades: Each new decade stepped lower. But how did single years behave inside those stair-steps?

annual.title: Below the Average
annual.description: Each bar shows how far a year finished above (blue) or below (red) the 1981 to 2010 average. Zero is that fixed reference, not the average of every year on the chart.
annual.analysis: Every year of the 1980s finishes above the line, on average 0.54 million km² above it. The 1990s wobble: nine years above, one below. From 2000 on, not a single year finishes above the reference.
annual.conclusion: The reference line does not drift with the data. It stays on the 1981 to 2010 average, the same line the decade chart uses. The bars are what moved.

drivers.intro: What is pushing the ice away? We have seen declining coverage and strong anomalies. Next, we put CO₂, global temperature, and Arctic temperature on the same scale.

connections.title: The Warming Signal
connections.description: Three lines, one story: global CO₂ emissions (green), global temperature (blue), and Arctic temperature (red) have climbed for decades.
connections.causation: The physical link is well established: more greenhouse gases trap more heat. In the Arctic, that warming shows up especially strongly.
connections.conclusion: The Arctic is an early warning system because regional change there connects back to weather, oceans, and climate elsewhere.

zscore.title: Apples to Apples
zscore.description: How do you compare CO₂ emissions (measured in tonnes) with temperature (degrees) and ice extent (square kilometers)?
zscore.method: By converting each series to the same kind of distance from its own historical average. Different units become comparable without pretending they are the same.

mirror.title: The Mirror Image
mirror.description: When we flip the ice-loss data upside down, the pattern becomes easier to compare: rising CO₂ and temperature move against falling ice.
mirror.conclusion: Three different measurements do not become the same thing. They become readable on the same scale.

chatbot.greeting: Greetings, traveller! I'm Knud Rasmussen, Danish-Greenlandic explorer and collector of Inuit legends. Ask me anything about the Greenlandic folktales I recorded in Eskimo Folk-Tales. Behind the scenes, modern technology helps me recall these stories clearly, blending the spirit of my journeys with today's AI.
chatbot.error: An error occurred. The spirits have gone silent. Please try again later.
chatbot.description: This chatbot is not Knud Rasmussen, and it was not trained on him. For every question it retrieves matching passages from “Eskimo Folk-Tales”, the collection of Greenlandic legends gathered by Danish-Greenlandic polar explorer Knud Rasmussen (1879–1933), and lets a language model (Claude Haiku 4.5 via OpenRouter) answer from them. Nothing is invented: what is not in the collection, it cannot tell.
chatbot.aboutKnud: Known as the 'Father of Eskimology,' Knud Rasmussen conducted groundbreaking expeditions across the Arctic from 1912-1924. Fluent in Greenlandic, he collected over 20,000 pages of Inuit oral traditions and stories of spirits, shamans, hunting, and Arctic life.
chatbot.folkTales: The 'Eskimo Folk-Tales' contain hundreds of stories: from Tulugaq the great raven who brought light to the world, to Sedna the sea goddess. These tales offer unique insights into the spiritual world of the Inuit.
chatbot.aiNote: Greetings, traveller. Ask me about specific legends, characters, or the meaning behind Arctic myths!

closing.lead: Listening is not the same as measuring.
closing.body: The satellites count the ice. The people of Uummannaq live with what its absence takes: routes, timing, trust, a way of being on the sea. The record here is nine years; the memory is a lifetime. Both point the same way.
closing.question: The future is unwritten. What we make of the measurement and the memory is the open question.
